utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And this is the case number, Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you, and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Anna Richterova and Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin. By the way, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you too, the three of you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am John Ackerman and I'm with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you as well. So any bad news before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You think every time I stand up it's bad news. I think, is it 1278 -- P1278? Is that the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the decisions of the Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a problem with regard to that document, Your Honour, that I have been discussing with the Prosecutor, and I just want to let you know what it is. For some reason, only parts of it were translated, so what you have is the full document in B/C/S, and just little parts of it in English. So that parts of it are in some ways unavailable for use in the courtroom. I'm not -- I'm not suggesting to you that I think we need to do anything about that except get it translated and get the exhibit brought up to where it needs to be as soon as possible. I've gone through it as best I can with the help of my assistants, and there are some parts of it that I would want to use but not necessarily with this witness. I can do it with some other witness. But it really needs to be made whole, and that's what we are doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need to have it translated in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. What is the exhibit? I mean, this is an exhibit that's supposed to be evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean to say is that I don't know how long it is in its original form because I only have the English version here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 92 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 92 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's 92 pages in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: See, I was wrong. 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not far off. And how much of it has not been translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, for example, decision number 18, 19, 20 has been translated. 21 hasn't. 22 has. 23, 24 have. 25 hasn't. 26 has. 27 hasn't. 28, 29, 30 have been translated. 31, 32, 33 have not. 34 has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Would you live with having this translated not officially?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As long as we have a record that reflects what's really going on. I mean, it's an exhibit. It ought to be complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there were instances previously where we agreed that given the resources of the Tribunal, to have it -- have some documents translated --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we -- that's not a problem. I don't care how it's done. Unofficially is fine with me. What we did earlier Your Honour I know with some one-page documents, we simply read it into the record. This is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Sutherland or Richterova, whoever is in charge of this, I think if we have a request for this document to be translated in its entirety, we'll have to accede to that request.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Last night the Prosecution found two documents, translations of two of the decisions contained within the Official Gazette, 2 of 1992, which aren't contained within Prosecution Exhibit 1268. We will request, if Mr. Ackerman requires, a draft translation of the other articles which haven't been yet translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you quite -- are you quite sure that this Official Gazette has not been translated, document hasn't been translated in its entirety in the Stakic case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I thought it had been, Your Honour, and I checked with the case manager in that case yesterday. And this is the only document that was submitted in the Stakic case as well. So for some reason, in my own mind, I thought that we had got the whole Official Gazette 2 of 1992 from the Prijedor Municipality translated, but it turns out it that it hasn't been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think probably the best way to do it Your Honour now is I stand here and think about it -- sit here and think about it is that I should actually take some time to go through it with my people here, because there is going to be some in there that really don't need to be translated. But there will be some that do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I suggested to you earlier whether it needs in reality to be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do it that way. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because to be frank with you, Mr. Ackerman, it does seem not odd, I mean, it's perhaps a strong word that I am using, or strange or whatever, but something to that effect, that the Defence teams in Stakic did not feel the need to have the rest translated, while in this case the need is being felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, both of the Defence counsel in Stakic speak the language, Your Honour. So they didn't need to have it translated. They can read it. And that's probably a small difference, but it is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, I just agreed if Mr. Ackerman wanted it translated. But upon reflection, I think that it's a waste of resources if there's a number of those in there that are totally irrelevant and I think if Mr. Ackerman wishes to flag to us which ones he wants translated, or he can get it done himself through the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman has already indicated this is precisely what he will do. Thank you Mr. Ackerman, thank you Ms. Sutherland. Shall we bring the witness in?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave you a memorandum today regarding the tapes. You asked me to give you the number of hours of tapes that Mr. Brdjanin needs to review. And I've done that as accurately as I can. I can't tell you it's a hundred per cent accurate, but I think it's very.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I also wanted information on documents that have been disclosed, transcripts --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That project is going on. There's two people at my office working on it right now. We'll be able to give you that material on Monday, I think, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Although the two are related obviously the approach must be different or needs to be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will continue, and we'll proceed and finish with your testimony today. And before you sit down, may I ask you to make -- repeat your solemn declaration to tell us the truth and the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland will finish with her examination-in-chief, and then Mr. Ackerman will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, in your Omarska testimony, and this is at page 5201, you stated that you were transferred from the Omarska camp to the Trnopolje camp. How long did you stay in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only stayed for a night and a day, which means I left the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you come to leave the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic, the camp commander, took me with his driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic, the camp commander of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so he came to the Trnopolje camp, and where did he take you?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took me to my flat, to my house, my family home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And from there -- you stayed how long?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed for a night and a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then I think in your Omarska testimony, you talk about going to Petrov Gaj?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's the village Zeljko Meakic comes from. My brother's wife's parents are from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Turning to another matter, yesterday in your testimony, you said that 43 people from the white house and 2 women, Sadeta Medunjanin and another woman were taken for a discharge. Do you recall when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the second half of July. It happened in July. They were sent for an exchange somewhere near Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what you've learnt about what happened to these people?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never got there. They never reached Bihac because supposedly, the exchange had failed, but they never returned them. They may have killed them somewhere along the road, but I wouldn't know really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1320.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this exhibit contains two documents, one dated the 8th of August, 1992, and the other dated the 16th of September, 1992. Could you review those documents to yourself. I'm sorry, I said one was dated the 8th of August. It is the 11th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at the first document dated the 11th of August, 1992, who is that -- who is that letter from?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a letter from the Bishop's diocese office in Banja Luka. It's a Catholic office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who is the signature block on the document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Franjo Komarica, the Bishop of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who is the letter addressed to?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's addressed to Simo Drljaca, chief of the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the letter is a request from Dr. Komarica in respect of one of his priests, Father Stipo Sosic. Do you see that in the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where in this letter it states that he is from Ljubija and that he has been in the Omarska camp since the 15th of June, 1992, and to date he has not received any information from Mr. Drljaca or any other competent authority about the priest.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at the second letter dated the 16th of September, 1992, is that a letter from the chief of the SJB, Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the letter from Mr. Drljaca informs the bishop that Mr. Stipo Sosic, the parish priest of Ljubija, was brought to the Omarska investigation centre on the 15th of June, 1992 because there were grounds to believe that he participated in the organisation of the armed rebellion against the Serbian Republic and the Serbian people, and that he stayed there until the end of the investigation on the 6th of August, 1992, when he was transferred along with other prisoners to the Manjaca military camp which is under the jurisdiction of the army of the Serbian Republic. Do you -- did you see father Stipo Sosic in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't personally see him but I know that people talked about him being there. Even before the war, he has been a very prominent priest because he had been contact with the politicians who were then in power, the communists. So he was not exactly anonymous, people in Prijedor knew about him and he was involved in the city's politics. I heard that he was in Omarska, but I didn't see him, and I knew from the other inmates stories that he had ended up in Omarska and indeed never got out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just going back to the first letter of the 11th of August, 1992, who were copies of the letter addressed to?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milomir Stakic, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor; General Talic in Banja Luka; and the papal nunciature in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, while you were detained in the glass house which you pointed out to Their Honours was part of the administration building in Omarska, were you ever told about a visit to the camp by a delegation from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were prepared for their arrival. I remember that one day, Brk passed through the restaurant and through the glass house and he said that those rooms should be tidied up and cleared up because an important delegation from Banja Luka would be arriving, including Brdjanin, Zupljanin, Radic, and some other names were mentioned, too. And when they would pass through, he told is to greet them with three fingers. I'm not sure why I was supposed to greet them like that. I suppose they liked it very much. Groups that were being taken for lunch were being trained to march, a march that was done in the former JNA. So if when the soldiers were treading, you only heard the tuck tuck sound. And the commander would say, "very well." And the answer was "we serve the people." And for that day, when the inmates were told "very well" they were supposed to answer was "long live Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a person called Brk. Who is that person, do you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the camp commander's driver. Officially, he was a driver, but he used to do other things, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when were you told that there was a delegation arriving?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of this delegation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in the second half of July, but I couldn't say for sure. Maybe the end of July, beginning of August. I'm not sure really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see the delegation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they passed outside the glass house and the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many people formed this delegation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large group of people. There were people from Prijedor there, there were bodyguards, police officers, military. There were some younger people wearing suits there. There were the police, the army. So I could only assume that those young men wearing suits were not politicians, but rather bodyguards. And then the policemen and the military. I think Simo Srdic was there, too. Simo Drljaca. I can't remember any other names. It has been ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The transcript reads Simo Srdic. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who did you recognise in the delegation from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I didn't really myself recognise, but I think the person walking at the head of this group was the one that was being paid the most attention to. And that was a rather short man wearing a dark suit, so I would have assumed that that would have been Brdjanin, the president of the autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to what he would have assumed. That's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who else -- was there anyone from Banja Luka that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were persons there who were from Banja Luka. I might have seen them in 1991 appearing on TV on some political talk shows, but not directly, not that I could really name any of them myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard of him as a politician before the war. He worked for the SDS, but I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Had you ever seen Mr. Radic on television?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Banja Luka TV. That was their TV. And mostly only their political leaders appeared on that TV station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who did you see from Prijedor in the delegation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I thought that Simo Srdic was there as well as Simo Drljaca, Milomir Stakic, Kovacevic, the elite. I don't think the entire Crisis Staff was there, but most of the Crisis Staff was. That is to say, from the president of the municipality to the secretary of the municipality, the commander of the police, the commander of security at the camp, and they were always the welcome committee before the war and during the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that Brk had mentioned Brdjanin as being part of this delegation that was going to visit the camp.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you mentioned a moment ago that you saw a short man leading the delegation who you assumed was Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You sustained the objection regarding that, Your Honour. It has been asked again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, when did you first see the person Brdjanin, who you referred to as the person Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He never said that he saw a person Brdjanin or referred to a person as Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will be more clear --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw him on television?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1991, the beginnings of the political parties and the election campaign and the elections. The second half of 1991, I think it was. Every day, or rather every night, this was debated, the Banja Luka politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What do you -- what was the nature of his -- of what you heard him say on the television?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like all other politicians favouring the greater Serbia, he also advocated the strengthening of the Serb Democratic Party, and in that framework already in the first half of 1991 it was no longer only the strengthening and promotion of the SDS, but also -- but in practice, promoting life in a single nation state. This started first in individual towns like Prijedor, but afterwards, it became just as cleansed as they had wanted it to be, and as they had promoted it. In the assembly in Sarajevo and everywhere else including Banja Luka through their henchmen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did what Mr. Brdjanin was saying make you feel?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only I. At first, we all thought that it was like a movie, an ugly movie, because it is repulsive that people who lived with you until that day, from that day onwards recognised you to be the enemy, and not just any old enemy, an enemy that you had to get rid of. And history showed that we were a people who simply had their hands in their pockets. I'm referring to non-Serbs. Individuals are individuals. Perhaps individuals should have been eliminated, but not in general terms, the entire population, not that everything and everybody that was not Serb had to be removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, I now want to turn to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1263.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who is the document -- what is the signature block on the document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President, Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is the title block on the top left-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Crisis Staff, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is handwritten below the date, the handwritten text?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For immediate delivery to the president of the municipal Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you please read the first paragraph and the first -- the first sentence and the first paragraph of the decision.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. The first sentence of the first paragraph or which first sentence, or the first sentence before it says "decision"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I wasn't clear. The first sentence before it says "decision."

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand. "At its meeting held on the 22nd of June, 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina adopted the following decision: All executive posts, posts involving a likely flow of information, posts involving the protection of public property, that is, all posts of importance to the functioning of the economy may only be held by personnel of Serbian nationality. "This applies to all socially-owned enterprises, share holding companies, state institutions, public service enterprises, ministries of the interior, and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "These posts may not be held by employees of Serbian nationality who have not confirmed by plebiscite or who in their minds are not ideologically clear that the Serbian democratic party is the sole representative of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see this decision at your work prior to your arrest on the 24th of June?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1174.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, this is the first of a number of documents I want to show you. I simply want to ask you whether you know the person named in this decision who is being dismissed from his post, and whether you know the person that was appointed to the position, and whether you know the fate of the person named as being dismissed. So this is a decision from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor dismissing Miroslav Turnusek from the post of director of the socially owned company Mira Cikota. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat. He was president of the committee of the league of communists, and his secretary was the other man underneath, Topic Ranko, who is an ethnic Serb, and he took his position in this cookie factory of Mira Cikota, which was within the factory of Josip Kras, Zagreb. He ended up in Omarska. He survived. I think he is in Zagreb now. I think he works as a director in Zbona [phoen]. He has a degree in chemistry. He worked as a chemistry teacher at the Prijedor high school before he was not engaged in politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1175 [sic]. For the record, Your Honour, P1174 is dated the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, again, this is another decision issued by the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor on the 2nd of May, 1992. And it's a decision dismissing Idriz Jakupovic from the post of president of the Prijedor municipal staff for the reception of refugees and appointing Jovan Vukoja to the post. Do you know Idriz Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him. He was director of the social welfare centre for many years before the war. He ended up in Omarska. First they broke his arm, either his left or his right arm. I can't say. Then he was taken in the direction of the red house. He never got out of Omarska. Jovan Vukoja, a teacher from the Rade Kondic elementary school, who worked with my father replaced him. I think he comes from Montenegro, but he is an ethnic Serb, an orthodox person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, just to clarify it, when he says "I think he comes from Montenegro but he is an ethnic Serb" he is referring to Jovan Vukoja. Can you tell us what was the ethnicity of Idriz Jakupovic, just to make sure that we are not confusing persons here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I should have asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, what was Idriz Jakupovic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is it correct that Jovan --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukoja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- Vukoja is from Montenegro and a Serb by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or Herzegovina, or Herzegovina. Perhaps is that area between Montenegro and Herzegovina. I'm not sure on which side of the border. I'm not sure. But he's an ethnic Serb at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1178. You've got that in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is another decision dated the 4th of May issued by the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. It's a decision dismissing Sabiha --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sabiha Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- from the post of secretary of the Prijedor Municipal conference of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know this woman?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally knew her.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim. She was married to the former president of the executive council, Obradovic was his last name. Sule was his nickname. They parted before the war. They had two children. Both sons were trained and were with the Serb army. One was doing his military service and other the one was on the reserve force. No, sorry. One son. It was this one son. I'm sorry, I got confused with another person. And the daughter was another person. Sabiha was in Omarska, survived, and is alive until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1181.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a decision dated the 4th of May, again, from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. It's a decision dismissing Esad Mehmedagic from the post of deputy municipal public attorney and appointing Slobodan Radulj to the post. First, do you know Esad Mehmedagic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. Because at first, he was a judge in the town of Prijedor, and then he was the municipal public attorney. He was a man who had trouble with his eyesight. He was almost blind. His wife drove him to court every morning, and he had to wait to be taken into the court house because he could not see. He ended up in Omarska, accused of being a sniper shooter. He was taken with Seric and Ago Sadikovic, who is my aunt's son-in-law. They were taken the same day in the direction of the black house. Slobodan Radulj, I know the name, I know the face. But I never met him in person. But I knew him by sight from town. Slobodan Radulj was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Seric and Ago Sadikovic and you said they were taken towards the black house, this was how it was translated to me.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I made a mistake. I actually wanted to say the red house, in the direction of the red house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This person that you mentioned, Seric, do you know his full name?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzad Seric is his name, judge of the municipal court in Prijedor. His wife was a Serb. He lived in a mixed marriage. He had two sons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of the elections commission during the March elections. When were the elections? In March 1992. He was president of the election commission. I think that's what this body was called, that the body that followed the election process in Prijedor from a judicial point of view or a legal point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Ago Sadikovic, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did either Esad Mehmedagic, Nedzad Seric, or Ago Sadikovic survive the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1188.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a decision dated the 5th of May, 1992, from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. It's a decision dismissing Vahid Ceric from the post of assistant commander for the organisation of mobilisation and personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me. I cannot hear interpretation into Bosnian, to my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure, usher, that he has not pressed the wrong number or moved the number. Then change his headphone, yes. Can you hear me now? Can you hear what I'm saying translated into Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear anything actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I hear you. Now I hear the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The problem seems to have been solved. Ms. Sutherland, sorry for that interruption. You've just referred the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reference Exhibit 1118, we are 1188. And that, incidentally, for the record, it's wrong in the transcript because you reported having said could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1118. In actual fact he is being shown supposedly P1188. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, do you have a document dated the 5th of May, 1992, with the number 02-111-62/92?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, 02-111-62/92. Yes. That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is a decision by the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor dismissing Vahid Ceric from the post of assistant commander for the organisation of mobilisation and personnel affairs?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it states that Major Radmilo Zeljaja shall be responsible for its implementation. First, do you know Vahid Ceric?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him very well. We cooperated. He worked at the TO headquarters and I worked at the secretariat for national defence. He was a Muslim, and at the same time he was the first victim of the authorities of the town of Prijedor, and he was taken to Stari Gradiska or some other camp, together with Fikret Kadiric, commander of the police station from earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know where he went after Stari Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ended up in Manjaca, and he's still alive. He survived the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Major Radmilo Zeljaja, yesterday you recognised him on a video that was shown to you. What was his post? What was his position? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him before the war, several years before the war. I can't remember exactly when because Bosko Deviak, Captain Bosko Deviak was in his place, but then he was transferred to a place near Foca. I know this because we worked together. Captain Bosko Deviak was in charge of the execution of the mobilisation and personnel affairs. That was the same post in the JNA, and then he was replaced by Radmilo Zeljaja, just as Colonel Muharem Efendic was also replaced by Lieutenant Colonel Arsic. So that's why I know Radmilo Zeljaja from the years before the war. He was a person I worked with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1189.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a decision dated the 5th of May, 1992, from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. It's a decision dismissing Jasminka Hadzibegovic from the post of deputy social attorney of self-management. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim. Trevo Hadzibegovic was her husband. I recognised him on the photograph yesterday -- no, not photograph. The video from the glass house. He and her brother, she was also in Omarska, deputy of Nona Samic, former teacher, and then before the war he was -- just a minute. He was deputy social attorney of self-management -- or rather, he was social attorney of self-management, and Jasminka was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1191. I'm sorry, 1191 and 1193.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First the decision P1191 is a decision dated the 7th of May from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. It's a decision relieving Dzemal Sefer as director of the PBS which is the commercial bank of Sarajevo main branch office in Prijedor. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at P1193, this is a ruling dated the 7th of May, 1992, from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. It's a ruling appointing Milan Nisevic as acting manager of the Prijedor main branch office of the PBS Privredna Bank of Sarajevo to the post. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What's his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb. For many years, he was president of the branch office of Investbanka [phoen] from Sarajevo in Prijedor. In 1975, 1976, I was president of the youth organisation in the part of town where I lived, and at the football club I was vice-president, and he was president of the Radnik football club.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1198.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a decision dated the 13th of May from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. It is a decision appointing Nikola Plemic as acting director the Borac work unit in Prijedor. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He replaced professor Vehbija Dzafic who had been taken to Omarska, and he survived the camp. He's still alive. Plemic Nikola is the father of Sale Plemic who went with me to the technical school in Prijedor. He was retired, and he was a Serb by nationality. He was a retired director of the Borac work unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So he was brought out of retirement to become acting director?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The professor that he replaced, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vehbija Dzafic was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Milan Niskovic, the Serb referred to in the last decision, was he retired or was he holding that post before he was given -- was he working or was he retired in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Niskovic was retired. I don't know exactly when he retired what year, but I think probably several years just before the war. He was an elderly person. I couldn't tell, he may be about 80 years old now, if he's still alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1201 and also P1200.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking first at 1201, it's a decision of the 13th of May, 1992 from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor dismissing Bozidar Bajic from the post of head of the department for economic and public services in the municipal secretariat for economic and public services. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Serb. He's a Serb who is married to a Muslim woman. First name Ramizi. I don't know her maiden name. She was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking now at Exhibit P1200, which is a decision of the 13th of May, 1992, from the executive committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor, it's a decision of appointing Ilija Ecim as acting head of the department for economic and public services in the municipal secretariat for economic and public services. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a Serb, and for a while he was the director of the Trg Proda [phoen] company in Prijedor. During the war or just before the war, he was in the municipality. I couldn't say which organ exactly, but he worked for the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1247.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a decision dated the 8th of June, 1992, from the acting director Ranko Sikman of the health services manager of the Dr. Mladen Stojanovic medical centre in Prijedor. It's a decision divesting Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, a specialist of internal medicine, of his duties as vice-president of the board of directors of the Dr. Mladen Stojanovic medical centre. Do you know this doctor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I used to know him. He ended up in Omarska. He had been brought to Omarska, and he never came out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim. A Muslim. He never got out of Omarska alive. Perhaps I should say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken towards the red house, as most of the others, but he wasn't there when the names were called out towards the end of July, and he did not attend lunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1284, and also P1292.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, this is an order dated the 2nd of July, 1992 with a signature block, president of the Crisis Staff, Milomir Stakic, and a signature. It is an order. Can you please read out the text of the order.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All organs, enterprises, and communities are ordered to terminate the employment of workers who have participated in the armed rebellion, and who are currently in Omarska and Keraterm. "Information about these workers is to be submitted by the Prijedor public security station on the request of the above-mentioned organs, enterprises, and communities. "The public security station and the competent municipal inspection service will be responsible for the execution of this order. "This order shall enter into effect on the day it is issued. "President of the Crisis Staff Milomir Stakic."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you look now at Prosecution Exhibit P1292. This is a document dated the 11th of July, 1992, signed by the chief of the public security station in Prijedor, Drljaca. And it's addressed to the work organisation, Dr. Mladen Stojanovic medical centre in Prijedor. Can you read the start of the document, re: verification of information-submitted. Could you read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Please find enclosed a list of your employees who are in some of the refugee camps in accordance with Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff order number 01-023-49/92 dated the 2nd of July, 1992, as follows:"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does it then name ten people under the heading "general hospital"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then it names seven people under "Prijedor health centre"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It also names one person under the pharmacy in Prijedor? I'm sorry, two people. One from the occupational medicine institute, and one from the work community Zajednicke Sluzbe?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at those names in Exhibit P1292, are you able to tell the Court the fate of any of the people named in that document? And if so, could you please give the name of the person, their ethnicity, and what you know happened to them.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bahonjic, Jakub Islam, I think he was an engineer, radiologist, something like that. An x-ray technician. He disappeared in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What's his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. Vehbija Ibrahim Beglerbegovic, a doctor, a Muslim, he only spent two days in Omarska. The inmates [as translated] of Omarska took him out of Omarska because he had been a doctor in the Omarska area for a long time so the locals got him out of the camp after two days, but his brother Rizo Beglerbegovic stayed behind. Esad Osman Crnkic I don't know him. Emir Aziz Blazevic I don't that man either. Meho Muharem Arnautovic, no. Omer Adnan Ekinovic, I don't know whether he was an x-ray technician or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could you give me the names of the people that you know of something that happened to them. The ones that are listed, if you can give me the number and where they appear on the document, under which heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt real quick, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's line -- page 27, line 1, what the witness said was the inhabitants of Omarska took him out of Omarska, not the inmates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will rephrase my last question. In relation to the people that are listed under the general hospital, you've mentioned something in relation to Islam Bahonjic and Ibrahim Beglerbegovic. Do you know any of those other people listed from numbers 3 to 10? Do you know any of those people?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, Bahonjic Jakub Islam, I've already said he was an x-ray technician or an engineer, I'm not sure. He was killed in Omarska. Number 2, Beglerbegovic Vehbija Ibrahim, a doctor, only spent two days in Omarska, and then the locals got him out of the camp, the inhabitants of Omarska. And then number 6, Ekinovic Omer Adnan, also an x-ray technician or an engineer, he worked with x-ray, he was killed in the white house. Neither he nor his father ever got out alive, and he was the best man at Slavko Ecimovic's wedding. That's what he was. Number 8, Sadikovic Hasib Esad, also a doctor, it was an organisation called Medecins sans Frontiere, I think that was the organisation he belonged to. He was taken from Omarska together with the people from Keraterm, and he never got back to us. I'll try with the Prijedor health centre now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pause there. Adnan Ekinovic, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim. Sadikovic Esad, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of the people listed under Prijedor health centre numbered 1 to 7, do you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have a look now. Harambasic Mujaga Hasiba, that's a woman. She was a dentist. Her nickname was Biba. She was a Muslim. She came to Omarska, and she survived. Balic Mahmut Uzeir, he was an accountant, he survived the Omarska camp, and he's alive today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is he number 4?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number 4. I apologise, number 4. He's a Muslim. I don't know the other names. I don't know their fate nor do I know the persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Under the heading "occupational medicine institute," do you know this person, Rufad Suljanovic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suljanovic Vejsil, a Dr. Rufad, he was killed. He was a Muslim. Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, I've talked about him already, and he too was killed. Actually, the only doctor to emerge from Omarska alive was Dr. Mensur Kursuran.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned that in your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is Dr. Sikora Zeljko missing from this list. Dr. Jusuf Pasic, Dr. Enis Begic. I can't remember any of the other ones now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This document is dated the 11th of July, 1992. If I can turn now to the last topic I wish to deal with. Can you be shown a document which doesn't have a Prosecution Exhibit number yet. And it can be given the next exhibit number, which is P1134. This was disclosed as Document 4.2148. Sir, this document is dated Pale, 17th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The block on the top left-hand corner reads: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina government commission for inspecting collection centres and other facilities for captives in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And this is a report of the commission on the inspection of collection centres and other facilities for captives in the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this document in the last few days prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we turn to the first page, it can be seen that the commission inspected facilities between the 10th and 15th of August as follows: Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm in Prijedor; Manjaca near Banja Luka; Krings in Sanski Most; and a secondary school centre and primary school in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did the majority of people leave the Omarska camp? You said you went to Trnopolje on the 6th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A group left for Trnopolje, and another group left for Manjaca on the same day. That was the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So approximately how many people, if you know, were in the group that went to Trnopolje, and how many people, if you know, were in the group that went to Manjaca approximately?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the figures really. I think two-thirds left for Manjaca and only one-third left for Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you aware of approximately how many people were in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 3.000 I would say, on average 3.000, with slight fluctuations up to 5 per cent. Those who were newly brought to the camp or those who had disappeared during the week. About 3.000. We counted the group in the glass house, a hundred people passed through on a daily basis -- a hundred groups passed through on a daily basis to get their lunch, and each group contained about 30 people. Of course, I'm not including the people who had been so badly beaten that they couldn't leave their accommodation, so sometimes they would steal a slice of bread and just take the slice of bread back to where those people lay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, when you left for Trnopolje and when the other group of people left for Manjaca, are you aware of anybody else that remained in the Omarska camp on the 6th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We thought there were about a hundred people there, perhaps a bit more, perhaps a bit less. But thereabouts, roughly a hundred. Perhaps more. I don't know the figure really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know how long they stayed in the camp for?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they stayed after we had left, and I don't know until when exactly they stayed. I had my own problems to worry about, where I should hide. And how I should take care of my family, so I really don't know, until what point in time those people stayed there, and there were several women in that group, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Turning to page -- the page with the ERN number 01245063. I think it's numbered 2 at the top of the page in your language, a document in your language.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you see the third paragraph down. I will read the paragraph to you. And the heading is "II, Omarska near Prijedor." The third paragraph reads: "The prisoners are kept in a hall containing military camp beds and orderly toilet facilities. Food is provided for them in the workers' canteen. The food is prepared in the mine's central building and is provided on a self-service basis. A first aid point is located in one of the offices and is staffed by a physician and a nurse to administer any first aid that may be required. While in more serious cases the prisoners are transferred to the medical centres in Banja Luka and Prijedor." First, did you sleep on a military-camp bed when you were in Omarska when you were detained there for six weeks?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of bedding were you provided with?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ceramic tiles. My group, the group that was staying where I was staying, we didn't have a roof over our head at all. For six weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The toilet facilities, were they orderly?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one where I was staying in the glass house, it was sort of tidy, because the guards used it. The guards and those who were with them. But this didn't happen on a daily basis. Popovic's shift, and Ranko, the electrician's shift, it wouldn't happen. So for 20 minutes you wouldn't be able to use it, because they refused to use the same toilet that we were using. That is, we were not allowed to use the same toilet they were using at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you were detained in the white house in the first couple of days when you arrived in Omarska. What were the toilet facilities in the white house?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning hours, we would just use the field, the meadow behind the white house. We would come out in groups of ten, only to pass water. We used a plastic jerry can, the top of which had been sawn-off to do the rest, at least during the three days that I spent in the white house. I once went to the toilet in the hangar which had been flooded, and it all came up to the surface. So there was -- it was flooded up to a height of 15 centimetres in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go to the toilet when you wished when you were in the white house?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We used a jerry can that was there to do it. During the night and most often, we stayed there because we had learned from those who had asked the guards to go to the toilet and they never came back, so we were gripped by fear of death which was stronger than our need to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, the food that was provided in the workers' canteen, were you able to access food on a self-service basis while you were detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We would take some bread and whatever was on the plate, we would take the bread, we would squeeze it for the liquid to be absorbed, and then it would come out. I never sat at a table and ate for six consecutive weeks, nor did most of the others in most of the cases. There was only one day the TV watching day, we would have beans. There was more beans than water on that day. But everything else you did in passing or in whichever room you were taken to. Lunch would be as brief as 13 or 14 seconds, and we had to do all of this running.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So how many meals a day were you provided?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One eighth of bread and whatever was on the plate and that was all we had for the whole day, and sometimes not even that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So that was once a day. So you weren't able to attend this self-service canteen whenever you felt like it to get food?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The first aid point which says in the following paragraph, a first aid point is located in one of the offices and is staffed by a physician and a nurse to administer any first aid that may be required. Do you recall there being a first aid point while you were detained in the Omarska?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So as we can see from the first page of this report, the inspection occurred between the 10th and 15th of August, 1992; and from what you have just testified to, that is after the 3.000-odd men and women had been transferred out of the camp. And you said that approximately a hundred or so people were left in the camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that document. Your Honour, I noticed the time. I was going to take the witness through the bundle of photographs to get him to identify a number of them. So I would like to do that, if I can, for five minutes after the break before the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfectly okay with us, I suppose. Mr. Ackerman? Okay, no problem. So we'll have a short break of 20 minutes, and then we will have the photos prepared for the witness. We are going to have a short break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, I now want to show you a number of photographs to see whether you can recognise what's in those photographs. The first photograph is ERN number 02123685. If that can be marked P1128-5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: .5. No, .6 it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because .5 was 9557.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also, 02123686, which can be 1128.7.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, looking at P1128.6, do you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the mosque. What its name? It's the minaret is on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And looking at P1128.7.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also the mosque, but viewed from a different angle. I think it's Donja Puharska, yes. Donja Puharska mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at the next photograph, ERN number 02123684, if that can be given P1128.8. Do you know -- do you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entrance reminds me of the Catholic church in Prijedor, but this photograph is -- well, I don't know. But at any rate, this reminds me of the entrance into the Catholic church in Prijedor near the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown P1128.3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: .3, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zarko Zgonjanin military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were the barracks situated?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is part of Urije, actually it belongs to Donja Puharska. It's on the road between Prijedor and Dubica, on the right-hand side. Sorry, let me just show this. These are the offices of the commander of the barracks. This part here was the mess and the kitchen, when the active-duty people were there, and then also up there were the dormitories when it was a recruitment centre. And then this is where active-duty officers had their offices. Because it wasn't a training centre any longer. 4777 was the unit that was there, and later on it was a motorised brigade. The building where I went, if not every other day, then at least once a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the next photograph, ERN number 0039-2311. If that can be given Exhibit Number P1128.9.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same building, the same building. There was yet another one here, another military post.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness will have to speak slower and give the numbers again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What's the name of that building again?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a small building here where two military post codes were, and they made up war units. That is to say, 2982 and 2346, both Partizan brigades. We spoke about that yesterday. So here in the yard were warehouses, and in the left-hand corner was the warehouse of the secretariat of national defence where the civil protection equipment was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that's the same as the other building, in the other photograph. The Zarko Zgonjanin barracks?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but it's a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the next photograph, ER number 0038-9747.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you sure of the number, Ms. Sutherland, because I -- 9747? Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It has got the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. This will be 1128.10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new elementary school in Trnopolje. This is where the library was. That's where my father worked towards the end of his life. That's where the school library was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph, ERN 0214-7092, which will be 1128.11.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Trnopolje again, and this building is the cultural centre. At first, it was for special events, and also it was used as a sports hall. This was the local commune, and then yesterday I told you about apartments for teachers, and that's where the old school was and where the store was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph, ERN 02147093, which will become P1128.12.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an extension of the other photograph. This is where the local commune was, and then the apartments of the teachers. That's where they were while the old school was still there in 1992. When I came here this is where the clinic was, where Dr. Idriz worked. I don't know his last name, and Azra Strikovic, who was the veterinarian. This part, as I already mentioned, I slept in this part. But this is the classroom where my father worked as a teacher 30 years before that, in the 1960s, so this was a great misfortune for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned the vet Azra Strikovic. Do you know what her maiden name was?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it starts with a B. Her sister Alma went to the technical school, but she was younger than me. She lived in Urije near my house. I can't remember. Her sister's name is Alma, and she is a mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph ERN number 02147091, which will become 1128.13.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Red Cross building where we got passes in order to get out of the Trnopolje centre under the patronage of the Prijedor Red Cross. This is the yard of the cultural centre that I referred to, and before the war, this was a small village cafe. I think Aika was the owner. This is where the Red Cross was, and this is where the office was where permits were issued to leave Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph, ERN 02006269, which will be 1128.14. And 02006265, which will be 1128.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what -- first of all, looking at P1128.14, do you know what's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And P1128.15. What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brick factory is behind this, yes, yes. I think that this is also the entrance into Keraterm. And behind it is the brick factory. My parents' house is somewhere around here about 500 metres away from here in the street of Dmitrije Tucovic. Was, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown photograph 01002416 which will be 1128.16.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is Keraterm, yes. Yes, it is Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a model that was constructed. Could the witness please be shown the next photograph, 01002444, which will be P1128.17.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is the same photograph that you picked out on P1.1 yesterday when you were shown --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- with the photographs around it.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph ERN 0040-9596, which will be P1128.18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Model of Omarska. The administrative building, the white house, the red house, and the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The administration building being the small building on the right as you're looking at the photograph; the hangar building being the big long red building to the left; the white house being the white building in the rear of the photograph; and the red house, the small building in the back left-hand corner. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph 02147090.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Ms. Sutherland, because I notice that on this photo, top right corner, there's already with reference to another case an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. We will have that -- we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to obliterate it or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We'll provide a fresh copy of that photograph. That should have been taken off before the photograph was reproduced. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Please take note of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next photograph is 02147090, which will become 1128.19.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Benkovac in Kozara, the road between Prijedor and Mrakovica. This is where the dormitories were, and this part here was the restaurant, and this here was the headquarters of the youth drive -- oh, I'm sorry for speaking so fast. These were the dormitories, and in this part, this is where the bathrooms and toilets were. You can't see it in this photograph. Here were dormitories as well. This building here was a restaurant with a kitchen, and then there was a clinic there, and then here was the headquarters of the youth work drives. No, sorry, this was for recreation, billiards, table tennis, et cetera. And this here was a stage. That is where the command of the youth work drive would go out and line up all the young people who came there to work. I don't know what this is out here because this is where the sports fields were. And then on the right-hand side, further to the right, there are soccer fields and also volleyball terrains.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the youth centre as we discussed yesterday was pre-1992?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was built in 1973 or 1974 because I was in high school then. I was just about to graduate when we worked up there. These were local youth work drives. It was closed sometime in the 1980s because there wasn't sufficient financial support.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next three photographs, 0039-2375, which will become 1128.20; and 0039-2397, which will become 1128.21; and 0039-2402 which will become 1128.22.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just briefly, looking at 1128.20, what is in that photograph? Where is this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Benkovac. This is the restaurant. This is the stage that I referred to already. To the left is the building of the headquarters, and this is where the clinic was. That's where young people who would have injuries would stay for a while, and then this is the restaurant where they had meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at the next photograph, 1128.21, where is that photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also Benkovac. These are the dormitories. This should be the clinic and the medical centre, and this should be the kitchen. And right here, here, is where the bathroom and the toilets should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Finally looking at 1128.22, where is that photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also Benkovac, and the dormitories. This is the headquarters that I referred to, and then dormitories, and then the restaurant down here, and then down there were the bathroom and toilets, and over here was the plateau for the lineup of the brigades and units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at the next photograph numbered 0039-6503 [Realtime transcript read in error "00396502"], which will be P1128.23, this is a still of the video that you saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say, Ms. Sutherland, 0039-6502?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, because in the transcript, it shows 0039-6502, and it needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, as I just said, that was a still taken from the video that was shown to you yesterday. Can you point to the people in the photograph that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Dr. Kovacevic. This is the person I didn't recognise yesterday either. And this is Simo Drljaca. And here in the corner is Nada Balaban. I remember from yesterday that she was wearing a pink shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So that is Kovacevic on the left, an unknown gentleman in the middle, Drljaca the third man, and the woman in the corner is Ms. Balaban?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph, 0039-4563, which will be 1128.24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simo Drljaca and Dr. Kovacevic. This is Dr. Kovacevic, and this is Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Kovacevic on the left and Drljaca on the right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Going back to -- I've finished with that photograph. Going back to the two photographs that you were shown of the mosque in Prijedor, P1128.6 and P1128.7, do you know when that mosque was damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the month of August, around midnight, or rather in the early morning hours after midnight, because I was in Petrov Gaj when two explosions occurred within ten minutes perhaps.
